questions.title: Foamy macrophages in the arterial wall
questions.question: The presence of many foamy macrophages in the arterial wall is characteristic of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Syphilitic (luetic) arteritis is an obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with plasma-cell–rich inflammation, not a foam-cell lesion.
explanations.B: Correct. Foamy macrophages (‘foam cells’) — lipid-laden macrophages in the intima — are the characteristic cells of ATHEROSCLEROSIS, forming the earliest lesion (the fatty streak) and populating the atheromatous plaque. They arise when intimal macrophages engulf oxidised LDL. Their presence in the arterial wall points specifically to atherosclerosis, not to syphilitic arteritis (plasma cells) or to hypertension (hyaline/fibrinoid arteriolar change).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypertension produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis or fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels, not collections of foam cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Because syphilitic arteritis and hypertension do not feature foam cells, ‘all of the above’ is wrong; foamy macrophages are characteristic of atherosclerosis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify foamy macrophages (foam cells) as characteristic of atherosclerosis, not syphilitic arteritis or hypertension.

questions.title: Most important complication of atherosclerosis
questions.question: The most important complication of atherosclerosis is:

explanations.A: Correct. THROMBUS FORMATION over a ruptured or ulcerated plaque is the most important complication of atherosclerosis, because it causes acute arterial occlusion and the major clinical events — myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke and acute limb ischaemia. Although plaques also ulcerate, calcify and weaken the wall into aneurysms, it is superimposed thrombosis that most often turns a chronic stable plaque into a lethal acute event. This is why plaque rupture with thrombosis dominates the mortality of atherosclerosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ulceration of the plaque surface occurs and can trigger thrombosis, but it is not itself the most important complication.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dystrophic calcification of plaques is common but is a marker of chronicity rather than the most important (life-threatening) complication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aneurysmal dilatation from medial weakening is an important complication (e.g. abdominal aortic aneurysm) but is less commonly the immediate cause of death than acute thrombotic occlusion.

questions.learning_objective: State that thrombus formation over a plaque is the most important complication of atherosclerosis.

questions.title: Cause of ischaemic heart disease in a smoker
questions.question: A 60 year old man who was a heavy smoker and not practicing exercise presented with ischemic heart disease. The most possible cause of this disease is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Valvular lesions cause haemodynamic overload and can secondarily reduce coronary flow, but they are not the usual cause of ischaemic heart disease in this risk profile.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Coronary embolism is a rare cause of myocardial ischaemia (e.g. from infective endocarditis or a mural thrombus), far less common than coronary atherosclerosis.
explanations.C: Correct. In an older heavy smoker with a sedentary lifestyle, ischaemic heart disease is overwhelmingly due to CORONARY ATHEROSCLEROSIS: atheromatous plaques narrow the coronary arteries and, on rupture with thrombosis, occlude them, producing angina and myocardial infarction. Smoking and physical inactivity are classic risk factors accelerating coronary atheroma. Atherosclerosis underlies the vast majority (about 90%) of ischaemic heart disease, which is why it is the most probable cause here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An aortic aneurysm is itself a consequence of atherosclerosis but is not the direct cause of ischaemic heart disease.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise coronary atherosclerosis as the usual cause of ischaemic heart disease in a smoker with cardiovascular risk factors.

questions.title: Medial calcification of arteries (Monckeberg)
questions.question: Medial calcification of arteries is seen in:

explanations.A: Correct. MÖNCKEBERG medial calcific sclerosis is defined by calcification of the MEDIA of medium-sized muscular arteries (classically the radial, ulnar, femoral and uterine arteries), typically in people over 50. The calcification is in the muscular media, does not narrow the lumen, and is usually clinically insignificant — the very definition of medial calcification of arteries being asked for here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Atherosclerosis calcifies the INTIMAL plaque, not the media; it is intimal (not medial) calcification.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum causes fragmentation and calcification of ELASTIC fibres (skin, retina, vessels), a different pattern from Mönckeberg medial calcification.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Idiopathic arterial calcification of infancy is a rare congenital disorder, not the classic ‘medial calcification of arteries’ intended here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis as the cause of medial (not intimal) calcification of muscular arteries.

questions.title: Clinically important changes in atherosclerotic plaques
questions.question: Atherosclerotic plaques are susceptible to following several clinically important changes:

options.A: Rupture, Hemorrhage into a plaque, atheroembolism, aneurysm formation.
options.B: Rupture, Hemorrhage into a plaque, atheroembolism, varicose vein formation.
options.C: Rupture, Hemorrhage into a plaque, air embolism, aneurysm formation.
options.D: Complete resolution, Hemorrhage into a plaque, atheroembolism, aneurysm formation.

explanations.A: Correct. Established atherosclerotic plaques undergo RUPTURE (fissuring/ulceration, often with overlying thrombosis), HAEMORRHAGE into the plaque (from fragile neovessels, rapidly enlarging it), ATHEROEMBOLISM (cholesterol/atheromatous debris embolising downstream), and ANEURYSM FORMATION (medial weakening beneath the plaque). All four are recognised clinically important complications of the plaque, so this is the correct combination.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Varicose VEIN formation is a venous disorder unrelated to arterial plaques; it does not belong in this list.
explanations.C: Incorrect. AIR embolism (gas entering the circulation) is not a plaque complication — the plaque produces atheroembolism (cholesterol debris), not air.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atherosclerotic plaques do NOT undergo complete resolution; they are progressive, so ‘complete resolution’ makes this option wrong.

questions.learning_objective: List the clinically important plaque complications: rupture, intraplaque haemorrhage, atheroembolism and aneurysm formation.

questions.title: Lesion presenting as acute myocardial ischaemia
questions.question: Which of the following lesions may be presented by acute myocardial ischemia?

options.B: Atheromatous plaque with lumen narrowing more than 75%.
options.D: Atheromatous plaque with excess fibrous tissue.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fatty streaks are the earliest, clinically silent lesion; they do not narrow the lumen enough to cause ischaemia.
explanations.B: Correct. Acute myocardial ischaemia requires a critically stenosing lesion: an ATHEROMATOUS PLAQUE narrowing the coronary lumen by MORE THAN ~75% (‘critical stenosis’) limits flow so that oxygen demand outstrips supply on exertion, producing ischaemia. Below this threshold flow is usually adequate at rest and even on moderate exertion, which is why the 75% cut-off is the classic teaching for flow-limiting coronary disease. (An acute event may then be precipitated by rupture/thrombosis of such a plaque.)
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer. Intraplaque haemorrhage can acutely enlarge a plaque and precipitate an event, but the lesion the question frames as causing ischaemia is the critically (>75%) stenosing plaque.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A fibrous (stable) plaque with excess fibrous tissue is the stable form; excess fibrous tissue alone does not define the ischaemia-producing lesion, which is the >75% stenosis.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a coronary atheromatous plaque narrowing the lumen by more than 75% (critical stenosis) causes myocardial ischaemia.

questions.title: Secondary changes in atheromatous plaques
questions.question: Secondary changes in atheromatous plaques include:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hypertrophy (increase in cell size) is not a secondary change of a plaque; plaques enlarge by lipid, smooth-muscle and matrix accumulation, not by cellular hypertrophy in this sense.
explanations.B: Correct. CALCIFICATION (dystrophic calcification of the lipid/necrotic core and fibrous tissue) is a classic secondary/complicated change in atheromatous plaques, along with ulceration, intraplaque haemorrhage, thrombosis and aneurysmal dilatation. Deposition of calcium salts into the degenerate plaque is common in advanced lesions and hardens the arterial wall. It is the only listed option that is a genuine secondary change of a plaque.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Metaplasia (change of one differentiated tissue type to another) is not a recognised secondary change in atheromatous plaques.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neoplastic change (tumour formation) is not a feature of atheromatous plaques.

questions.learning_objective: Identify calcification as a secondary (complicated) change in atheromatous plaques.
